newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Lonrho works on split-up, profits rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lonrho works on split-up, profits rise.

text.p: Conglomerate Lonrho Plc, announcing a 12.6 percent rise in full-year profits, said on Thursday its long-mooted break-up plan had not been derailed by a European Union investigation involving the company.
The widely-diversified company said it remained committed to breaking up its mining and African trading business after the planned sale of the Princess hotel chain had been completed.
The EU recently began probing a 28 percent stake in Lonrho acquired by South African mining giant Anglo American.
The EU has barred Anglo from voting its Lonrho shares pending its investigation into possible competition complications due to their interests in platinum.
"It (the probe) won't stop me from going to shareholders and asking them for permission to do something in terms of a demerger or a sale," Lonrho's chief executive Nick Morrell said.
Together with South African rival Gencor, Anglo and Lonrho control about 60 percent of the world output of platinum, used in car exhaust catalysts.
Lonrho plans to stick to the precious metal operations after the EU earlier barred Lonrho from merging its platinum activities with Gencor. The South African company is still fighting the decision.
But Lonrho said it would ignore the EU problems and simply stick to its platinum operations.
"We intend to make our future as an independent company producing platinum. What that does to Anglo or Gencor is not Lonrho's issue," Morrell told Reuters in an interview.

A demerger was the preferred way to streamline the company's operations but regulatory hurdles could eventually put a spanner in the works and necessitate a straightforward sale of the non-mining assets, he said.

There may even be a combination of a demerger and a divestment, he said. "Whether we can achieve a demerger, I don't yet know, but I think it is the obvious route for giving shareholders maximum value," Morrell added.
Lonrho, which saw pre-tax profit before exceptional items rise to 170 million pounds ($285 million) from 151 million last time, first announced its break-up plans a year ago.
But after several delays and adjustments, the only step taken so far has been the October sale of its Metropole hotel chain to Britain's Stakis Plc.

Morrell said he hoped to conclude the Princess divestment and the ensuing demerger as soon as possible, but declined to be Lonrho's results for the year to September 30 were boosted by improved performances of its hotels, and its agricultural and other trading operations.
But the profit rise, which was bigger than analysts had expected, was dampened by lower mining results, which were hit by falling mineral prices and devaluation of the rand, Lonrho said.
Shares in Lonrho firmed two pence to 127 pence in late morning trading. ($1=.5976 Pound)
